candidates.title: Check the gauge’s volume-to-rainfall conversion
candidates.proposal:
Test whether the gauge itself loses water or reports the wrong depth. This approach needs a measurable collector opening and readable cup markings; it uses rainwater retained from the first event, with no added equipment or water supply.

Before event 1, sketch the location and note visible cracks, blockage, obvious leaning, nearby shelter and the gauge’s units. Empty it and read subsequent rainfall at eye level, consistently using the same part of the meniscus. After recording event 1, retain its water in the marked cup. During a dry interval, slowly return a measured volume through the normal collector without splashing. For a circular opening of diameter D centimetres, area A = πD²/4 square centimetres; V millilitres should represent 10V/A millimetres of rainfall. Use the opening area, not the narrower measuring tube’s area. If the opening geometry or cup graduations are unclear, treat the result as approximate.

Compare expected and indicated depth at two available volumes, then inspect whether the reading falls during a rain-free observation interval. Repeat a suspect result to check pouring and residual-water effects. Empty the gauge before event 2. During events 2 and 3, use the same reading procedure and compare totals only with public reports covering matching periods. A repeatable conversion error or water loss supports a measurement explanation; a successful check leaves exposure, timing and actual spatial variation unresolved.
candidates.experiment: Use calculated depth as the comparator, allowing for cup divisions, ruler precision and gauge divisions. Agreement at two volumes and stable retained water weakens the calibration/leak explanation. Repeated disagreement supports it but requires checking the pour itself. This does not reproduce wind-driven collection losses, and three events cannot establish that the public station represents the garden.

candidates.title: Use the marked cup in a simultaneous location crossover
candidates.proposal:
Test whether the gauge’s surroundings reduce its catch by collecting rain simultaneously at two accessible ground-level locations. Choose its usual position A and a more open garden position B, away from roof runoff and obvious splash. Use the site sketch to record nearby shelter. Both vessels must stand securely without added supports, and the cup must have an unobstructed opening and enough capacity. If those conditions fail, this route is unsuitable.

Measure both opening areas with the ruler. For each vessel, collected volume V millilitres over opening area A square centimetres corresponds to 10V/A millimetres. Use the gauge’s normal scale for its primary reading. After an event, its water can be measured in the cup as a rough check of that scale, provided the cup has already been read and emptied. Cup graduations and retained droplets limit precision.

For event 1, put the gauge at A and the cup at B. For event 2, exchange their positions. For event 3, repeat event 1’s arrangement. Place and empty both before rain, read both after the same collection interval, and reset between events. Record overflow, splash, disturbance, rain direction and visibly different storm conditions. Compare depth per opening area, never raw volumes.

A lower catch that follows position A through the exchange supports an exposure effect. A lower catch that follows the gauge supports an instrument-specific effect. Similar garden readings with a differing, time-matched public report are compatible with local rainfall variation, while leaving shared collection errors possible.
candidates.experiment: Compare the simultaneous A/B depth ratios across all three events. A position effect should survive the vessel exchange; reversal with vessel identity weakens that explanation. Different wind conditions can change shelter effects, so an inconsistent crossover remains inconclusive. The cup is an imperfect comparator, not a reference instrument; skip this route if its geometry, stability or overflow prevents interpretable collection.

candidates.title: Reconcile collection periods before interpreting rainfall differences
candidates.proposal:
Test whether the apparent undercount comes from comparing an event total with a differently timed public daily total. This route works best when the public report states its accumulation cutoff and the garden can be observed safely at corresponding boundaries. It requires no second collector or relocation.

Before the first event, inspect the gauge for blockage, damage, obvious leaning and unreadable markings. Note units and the public report’s date convention, cutoff and rounding. Establish an empty-gauge baseline at a matching reporting boundary before event 1. Through the next three rain events, record garden readings at matching boundaries whenever feasible, plus observations of rain starting, stopping or continuing across a boundary. Empty only after recording each interval. Never visit during unsafe weather; mark a missed boundary as uncertain rather than assigning rainfall to a guessed day.

Compare garden and public totals first over matched daily intervals, then over the complete shared interval covering all three events. Include intervening dry days and any rain within that interval; do not sum only selected public wet days. Keep readings in millimetres and retain the original values before rounding. Note any overflow, delayed collection or unobserved rain.

If individual daily deficits are offset by excesses on adjacent days and the shared-interval totals agree within reading precision, timing is a plausible explanation. If a deficit persists over the complete matched interval, timing alone is insufficient. To check a gross instrument fault, retain event water and perform a measured-volume return through the collector using its opening area; persistent disagreement or declining retained water supports measurement error. A passing check leaves exposure and spatial variation as competing explanations.
candidates.experiment: Use the original event-versus-daily comparison as the simple comparator. Ask whether matching boundaries and summing the shared interval removes the apparent deficit. Persistence falsifies a timing-only explanation. Unknown public cutoffs or missed garden boundaries prevent a decisive test. This route does not measure exposure losses or independently establish the garden’s true rainfall.
